summary: Describes using AES in Cipher Block Chaining mode, with an explicit initialization vector, to provide confidentiality in IPsec ESP. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says how to encrypt an IPsec packet with AES, the modern replacement for DES. The important detail is the initialization vector: a fresh random number is generated for every packet and sent in the clear at the front of the encrypted data, so that two packets with the same contents do not produce the same encrypted bytes.

subtitle: How to use AES in CBC mode, with a fresh random IV in every packet, to encrypt IPsec ESP traffic.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs an encryption algorithm, and the older DES was due to be replaced.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies AES, the cipher NIST chose after an open competition, used in Cipher Block Chaining mode inside ESP. Every packet carries its own random 16-octet initialization vector, which is XORed with the first block of plaintext.
tldr.outcome: The RFC assigned the IANA identifiers that let two ends negotiate AES-CBC, and it was intended to become the default ESP cipher.

facts.label: IV size in the ESP payload

today: RFC 3602 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It specifies AES in CBC mode for IPsec ESP, and it assigns the identifiers that let two ends negotiate the cipher.

sections.title: Why AES, and Why in CBC Mode
sections.content:
After a four-year open competition with public participation and comment at each step, NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) selected AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard, as the successor to DES. The cipher, formerly known as Rijndael, was chosen from a field of five finalists. It was selected for its security, because it is unclassified and publicly disclosed, because it is available royalty-free worldwide, because it handles a block size of at least 128 bits and key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits, because it is computationally efficient in software and hardware including smart cards, and because it is simple and easy to implement. The expectation in the document is that AES will be the government's designated encryption cipher and will be widely adopted by businesses and financial institutions.

The intention of the IETF IPsec Working Group was that AES would eventually be adopted as the default IPsec ESP cipher and would obtain the status of a requirement that compliant IPsec implementations include it.

For the mode of operation, NIST has defined five modes for AES and other FIPS-approved ciphers: CBC (Cipher Block Chaining), ECB (Electronic CodeBook), CFB (Cipher FeedBack), OFB (Output FeedBack) and CTR (Counter). This document specifies AES in CBC mode within ESP. CBC is well defined and well understood for symmetric ciphers, and at the time it was already required for the other ESP ciphers. CBC needs an initialization vector the same size as the block size, and using a randomly generated IV prevents identical ciphertext being produced from packets with identical data that spans the first block of the cipher's block size.

Mechanically, the IV is XORed with the first plaintext block before it is encrypted. For each block after that, the previous ciphertext block is XORed with the current plaintext, and the result is encrypted.
sections.plainLanguage: AES is the encryption algorithm the United States government chose after an open contest, and this RFC says how to use it inside IPsec. It uses a method called cipher block chaining, where each block of the message is combined with the encrypted block before it, so that a change anywhere in the message changes everything after it.

sections.title: Key Sizes, Rounds and Padding
sections.content:
AES supports three key sizes: 128, 192 and 256 bits. The default is 128 bits, and every implementation must support that size; implementations may also support 192 and 256 bits.

The cipher uses a different number of rounds for each key size. With a 128-bit key an implementation must use 10 rounds, with a 192-bit key 12 rounds, and with a 256-bit key 14 rounds.

Some ciphers have weak keys, keys that must not be used because of how they interact with the cipher's definition. At the time of writing there were no known weak keys for AES. If weak keys are discovered later, they should be checked for and discarded when using manual key management; with dynamic key management such as IKE, weak key checks should not be performed, since they are seen as unnecessary added complexity that could weaken the intended security.

AES uses a block size of sixteen octets, or 128 bits. Padding is required to maintain that block size, and it must be added, as specified in the ESP specification, so that the data to be encrypted, which includes the ESP Pad Length and Next Header fields, has a length that is a multiple of 16 octets. Because of that requirement no additional padding is needed to make the ciphertext end on a 4-octet boundary, since keeping the 16-octet block size guarantees that the Pad Length and Next Header fields are right aligned within a 4-octet word. Additional padding may be included, as long as the 16-octet block size is maintained.
sections.plainLanguage: AES works on blocks of sixteen bytes at a time, and the packet has to be padded out to a whole number of blocks. The key may be 128, 192 or 256 bits long, and a longer key means more rounds of the cipher.

sections.title: The ESP Payload
sections.content:
The ESP payload is made up of the initialization vector followed by the raw ciphertext. The IV field must be the same size as the block size of the cipher being used, it must be chosen at random, and it must be unpredictable.

Including the IV in each datagram means that each received datagram can be decrypted on its own, even when some datagrams are dropped or reordered in transit. To avoid CBC encryption of very similar plaintext blocks in different packets, implementations must not use a counter or other low-Hamming-distance source for IVs.

The RFC also notes that there are currently no known issues in the interaction between AES and other aspects of ESP, such as the use of certain authentication schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each encrypted packet starts with sixteen bytes of random data that are sent unencrypted. The receiver needs them to work out what the first block of the message was, and because they are different every time, the same message encrypted twice does not look the same twice.

sections.title: Keying Material
sections.content: The minimum number of bits sent from the key exchange protocol to the ESP algorithm must be greater than or equal to the key size. The cipher's encryption and decryption key is taken from the first x bits of the keying material, where x is the required key size.
sections.plainLanguage: The key that both ends agree during the key exchange has to be at least as long as the AES key, and the cipher takes the part of it that it needs.

sections.title: Negotiating AES-CBC with IKE
sections.content:
IANA has assigned an Encryption Algorithm ID of 7 for AES-CBC in Phase 1 negotiations, and an ESP Transform Identifier of 12 for ESP_AES in Phase 2 negotiations. Because AES allows variable key lengths, the Key Length attribute must be specified in both a Phase 1 exchange and a Phase 2 exchange, so that both ends agree on how long the key is.

The RFC also discusses the hash algorithm used alongside the cipher. A companion competition to choose a successor to SHA-1 had recently concluded, and the resulting hashes, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, can produce output of 256, 384 and 512 bits, which is enough to generate and to authenticate the three AES key sizes. However, HMAC-SHA-1 and HMAC-MD5 were then considered of sufficient strength to serve both as IKE generators of 128-bit AES keys and as ESP authenticators for AES encryption using 128-bit keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers let the ends of a secure tunnel agree to use this cipher, one for the first stage of the key exchange and one for the second. Because the key can have three different lengths, both ends must also say in the exchange how long it is.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC gives eight test cases. The first four test AES-CBC encryption, and each gives a key, the plaintext and the resulting ciphertext. Values of keys and data are either hexadecimal numbers, prefixed by 0x, or ASCII character strings in double quotes. When a value is an ASCII string, the computation does not include the trailing null character of the string, and the computed ciphertext values are all hexadecimal numbers.

The last four cases are sample ESP packets using AES-CBC, in transport mode and in tunnel mode, and all their data are hexadecimal numbers without the 0x prefix. The first of them shows a transport-mode ESP packet carrying a ping, listing the IP header and the data of the original packet, the padding, the pad length and next header that were added, the pre-encryption data, and then the post-encryption packet with its SPI, sequence number, IV and encrypted data.

These test cases were verified with two independent implementations: the NIST AES-CBC reference implementation and an implementation provided by the authors of the Rijndael algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes worked examples with fixed keys, inputs and outputs, so that anyone writing an implementation can check it produces exactly the same bytes. The later examples are complete encrypted packets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations are encouraged to use the largest key sizes they can, taking account of performance considerations for their particular hardware and software configuration. Encryption necessarily affects both sides of a secure channel, so the choice has to take the client and the server into account, not one side only. A key size of 128 bits is nevertheless considered secure for the foreseeable future.

For more information about the necessary use of random IV values, the reader is pointed to the referenced work on probable plaintext cryptanalysis of the IP security protocols, and for further security considerations to the AES specification itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Longer keys cost more work on both ends of the connection, so the size is a choice each deployment makes. The RFC says a 128-bit key is enough for the foreseeable future, as long as the random numbers used with it really are random.
